titre: Three Independent Laboratories Date the Shroud of Turin by Carbon 14
accroche: In 1988, three laboratories date the same fragment of the Shroud of Turin, with fabrics of known age as controls, without comparing their results.
contenu_vulgarise:
A carbon 14 dating first gives a number, then a doubt: the method does not measure an exact age, but the amount of carbon 14 that remains in a fabric, which decays at a known rate, and converts it into a range of dates with a probability attached. On an object as disputed as the Shroud of Turin, that range could convince only if the measurement itself was shielded from suspicion.

## The mechanism

After several years of negotiation with the Holy See, the final protocol is published in Nature in April 1988 by Michael Tite, of the British Museum. Three laboratories, Oxford, Zurich (the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology) and Tucson (Arizona), will each receive a sample taken from a single place on the cloth, along with control samples of already known age, and must not compare their results before they are certified. The sampling takes place in April 1988, in Turin. The fragment is packaged by Tite and the archbishop, out of the presence of the laboratories’ representatives.

An initial plan, known as the Turin protocol (1986), called for a blind test, with indistinguishable samples. It is abandoned: the Shroud’s herringbone weave could not be reproduced in the controls, so a laboratory could have recognized the Shroud sample anyway. The three teams measure by accelerator mass spectrometry, a technique that directly counts carbon 14 atoms rather than waiting for them to decay.

The result, published in Nature on February 16, 1989, under the names of twenty-one authors, is clear: “The results provide conclusive evidence that the linen of the Shroud of Turin is mediaeval.” The calibrated range, 1260 to 1390 CE at a 95% confidence level, matches the documented history of the Shroud, which begins in 1354 with its exhibition in the collegiate church of Lirey, in France.

## The shift

The debate did not stop in 1989. In 2005, the chemist Raymond Rogers claims that the sample contained a coating of gum, dye and mordant as well as cotton fibers, absent from the rest of the Shroud, which he interprets as the trace of a medieval repair. The provenance of the threads he analyzed remains uncertain, however. Statistical reanalyses of the measurements (Riani and colleagues in 2013, Walsh and Schwalbe in 2020) point to a lack of homogeneity among them. Walsh and Schwalbe note that the three controls show none, and that an offset on the order of ten radiocarbon years would be enough to restore it, without the cause being established. Experts continue to hold the dating to be valid, and the public debate goes on.

What the episode teaches does not depend on the outcome of that debate. A carbon 14 measurement is worth only as much as its protocol, and a protocol is negotiated: here, the blind test was set aside for a technical reason, and it was through other safeguards, several independent laboratories, controls of known age, packaging out of the presence of the laboratories, that the result was made solid. Without these safeguards, no range of dates, even one published in a scientific journal, would prove much on its own.

carte.punch: Three laboratories date the Shroud to the Middle Ages. The planned blind test had been dropped.
carte.idee: In 1988, the laboratories of Oxford, Arizona and Zurich each date a fragment of the Shroud, with fabrics of known age as controls. Their result, published in Nature in 1989, comes down to a single range: 1260 to 1390, at 95% confidence.

quiz.question: Why did the final 1988 protocol give up the blind test planned at the outset?
choix: Because the Shroud’s herringbone weave could not be imitated in the controls, and a laboratory would have recognized the sample anyway
Because accelerator mass spectrometry requires the laboratory to know the sample’s presumed age
Because the laboratories had themselves taken the fragment from the cloth and knew where it came from
Because none of the plans discussed before 1988 had ever considered a blind test
quiz.explication: The 1986 Turin protocol called for indistinguishable samples, but the final 1988 protocol gave this up: the Shroud’s herringbone weave could not be reproduced in the controls, so a laboratory could recognize the Shroud sample. The other three options are false: the method does not require knowing the presumed age, the fragment was taken in Turin by people other than the laboratories, and the blind test was indeed part of the 1986 plan.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a carbon 14 dating given with a 95% confidence level mean?
choix: That it designates a range of dates, not a single certain date
That the measurement is accurate to within 95%, in years
That 95% of the sample’s carbon 14 atoms were counted
That the method works on 95% of the fabrics tested
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Carbon 14 never delivers a single date but a statistical range, here 1260-1390, with a confidence level attached. The other three options confuse this confidence level with a precision in years, an atom count or a success rate of the method.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly is the hypothesis put forward by Raymond Rogers in 2005?
choix: That the sample dated in 1988 came from an area repaired in the Middle Ages, rich in materials absent from the rest of the cloth
That the three laboratories had used different calibration standards
That the Shroud had been deliberately aged by chemical treatment in the 19th century
That fungal contamination had skewed all the measurements
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rogers claims that the sample contained a coating of gum, dye and mordant as well as cotton fibers, absent from the rest of the Shroud, and sees in it the trace of a medieval repair. The provenance of the threads he analyzed is uncertain, however. The other three options do not match his hypothesis as reported.
